paras: The killing of William Dempsey took place in January 1888 near the mouth of Grapevine Creek in Logan County, West Virginia, when an armed party from Pike County, Kentucky, fired on a Logan County constable's posse in which Dempsey was serving. Dempsey was shot dead, and two accounts said he was finished off with a shot to the head as he lay wounded and pleading. The killing drew national coverage as part of the Hatfield-McCoy feud and led to indictments and rewards for the Kentucky party.

Earlier in January a party of Kentuckians led by Frank Phillips had crossed into Logan County and killed James Vance, according to West Virginia sources. Warrants for six of the party went to Constable J. R. Thompson, who summoned a guard of thirteen men, Dempsey among them.

According to the Catlettsburg dispatch, a twenty-man "capturing party" from Pikeville crossed the Tug River and near Capt. Hatfield's house was fired on by eight Hatfields, who wounded Bud McCoy. Returning fire, the party brought down "Will Dempsey, of the Hatfield gang," shot through the bowels. As Dempsey lay dying and begging to be spared, the dispatch said, "the man that killed Jim Vance on the first raid" put a gun to his head and fired.

W. P. Floyd, a member of Thompson's guard, wrote on January 22 that about thirty men with Winchester rifles fired on the posse near the mouth of Grapevine from behind a fence, and that a later volley killed Dempsey, hitting him three times. Governor E. W. Wilson, writing to Kentucky's governor on January 26, likewise said Dempsey was killed "while acting as a deputy" by thirty or forty armed men from Kentucky.

A New York Sun retrospective that October had thirteen "Logan Regulators" open fire on Jim McCoy, who shot Dempsey. The Kentuckians tracked the unarmed Dempsey to a shuck pen, where, as he begged not to be shot again, Frank Phillips shot him through the head.

Logan County residents held a mass meeting and sent Floyd and J. A. Sheppard to Charleston with a petition asking for troops on the border. Wilson sent an agent to Logan County and ordered sixty men there, then countermanded the order when the agent reported both sides disbanded.

In June 1888 Wilson offered rewards for Pike County men indicted in Logan County for killing Vance and Dempsey: $500 for Frank Phillips and $100 each for twenty-six others. No report of an arrest or trial for Dempsey's killing appears in the coverage.

The first word came from the Kentucky side, in a Catlettsburg special sent through Cincinnati on January 24 that ran within two days in Washington, Alexandria, Wheeling, New York, St. Paul, Fort Worth and Indianapolis. It cast Dempsey as a Hatfield and his killers as a posse, yet called the head shot an "inhuman and sickening act." Headline writers read it as a story of murder: the Washington Evening Star called the feudists "As Savage as Apaches," the St. Paul Daily Globe announced the "Brutal Murder of One Man," and the Fort Worth Gazette said Dempsey was "Brutally Murdered While Begging for Mercy." The Waterbury Evening Democrat ran a rewritten version headed "Citizens Take a Hand," describing the vendetta as "going bravely on."

West Virginia papers pushed back. The Wheeling Register put the wire under its own headline "The Kentucky Gang Invade Logan County," then printed Floyd's letter as "The Hatfield Side," calling the wire "erroneous." In June the Big Sandy News of Louisa, Kentucky, reported the rewards with the remark that Wilson had been "defeated" in the court "bouts."

Floyd's letter, written a day after the fight by a posse member, mentions only a volley, but the Sun's later account agrees with the wire on the head shot and names Phillips as the shooter. The date is given as Saturday (January 21) by the wire and the Charleston report, "the 22d" by a later Charleston report, and "last Thursday" by the governor. Bud McCoy is described as wounded, dying, or killed, and the governor's agent said an unnamed second man died with Dempsey.

reader.title: Killing of William Dempsey
bases: A Kentucky armed party that the Catlettsburg wire called a 'capturing party' and 'posse' shot William Dempsey, a member of a West Virginia constable's posse, and by two accounts killed him with a shot to the head after he lay wounded (A2, A11, A17, A23); West Virginia sources deny the party had any lawful authority (A15).

The Kentucky wire, a letter from a member of Dempsey's posse, the West Virginia governor's letter, his agent's report and a later New York account independently agree that Dempsey was shot dead in a clash between the Kentucky party and a Logan County posse (A2, A11, A15, A17, A23), though they disagree on his role and how he died.

accounts.label: Kentucky (Catlettsburg) wire
accounts.gist: A twenty-man Pike County capturing party was fired on by eight Hatfields; returning fire, it shot 'Will Dempsey, of the Hatfield gang' through the bowels, and the man who had killed Jim Vance then put his gun to the dying man's head despite his pleas.

accounts.label: Posse member's letter (W. P. Floyd)
accounts.gist: Constable Thompson's thirteen-man guard, serving warrants for Vance's killers, was fired on near the mouth of Grapevine by about thirty men behind a fence; after a half-hour fight a second volley killed Dempsey, hit three times.

accounts.label: Governor Wilson
accounts.gist: Dempsey was killed while acting as a deputy under a warrant for Frank Phillips and others, by thirty or forty armed Kentuckians who fired on the posse.

accounts.label: Governor's agent
accounts.gist: The party that killed Vance invaded again and fired on Constable Thompson and posse, killing Dempsey 'and another man'.

accounts.label: New York Sun retrospective
accounts.gist: Thirteen Logan Regulators opened fire on Jim McCoy, who shot Dempsey; the Kentuckians tracked the wounded, unarmed Dempsey to a shuck pen, where Frank Phillips shot him through the head as others tried to stop him.

framing.detail: The Catlettsburg wire ran as 'War of Extermination' and similar heads in Alexandria, Washington, New York, St. Paul, Fort Worth and Indianapolis, casting Dempsey as a Hatfield and the shooters as a posse while calling the head shot 'inhuman and sickening'.

The Wheeling Register put the Kentucky wire under 'The Kentucky Gang Invade Logan County ... Murdered in Cold Blood', then printed 'The Hatfield Side' and 'Kentucky Outlaws', treating the Kentuckians as invaders resisting arrest.
The Waterbury Evening Democrat headed its version 'Citizens Take a Hand. Putting an End to the Hatfield-McCoy Feud with Rifle and Bullet' and said the vendetta was 'going bravely on'.
The Big Sandy News (Kentucky) reported the West Virginia rewards with a jibe that Wilson had been 'defeated' in the court 'bouts'.

record_check.dossier: posse_killing: one man of a constable's posse shot by a Kentucky armed party styled a 'capturing party'; not an attack on a community.
West Virginia is supported; the summary's doubt about the Kentucky side is not borne out: the posse member, the governor and the Sun all place it in Logan County, W. Va.
Jan. 21 (Saturday) is the best-supported date; other reports give the 22d, Thursday the 19th, or about the 18th.
A Pike County party of twenty to forty under Frank Phillips, called a posse by the Kentucky wire and a gang or marauders by West Virginia sources.
Frank Phillips's Kentucky party; the head shot attributed to Phillips (Sun) or to 'the man that killed Jim Vance' (wire).
1 named (Dempsey); one report says another man was also killed, and Floyd says Bud McCoy was killed.
None against Dempsey; his posse was serving warrants for Vance's killers.

info: Saturday before Jan. 24, 1888 (Jan. 21) per the Catlettsburg wire and the Charleston report of Floyd's letter; 'the 22d' per a later Charleston report; 'last Thursday' (Jan. 19) per Governor Wilson's Jan. 26 letter; the Sun's retrospective has the party reaching West Virginia on Jan. 18.
Near the mouth of Grapevine Creek on the Tug River, near Capt. ('Cap') Hatfield's house.
William (Will, Bill, W. D.) Dempsey, killed; race not stated. Bud McCoy of the Kentucky party wounded (or killed, per Floyd's letter). One report says 'another man' was killed with Dempsey.
No accusation against Dempsey; the Kentucky wire labels him 'of the Hatfield gang', while West Virginia sources call him a deputy or posse member serving warrants.

A party from Pike County, Kentucky, led by Frank Phillips, which the Kentucky wire calls a 'capturing party' or 'posse' and West Virginia sources call a 'gang', 'marauders' or 'outlaws'; the head shot is attributed to 'the man that killed Jim Vance' (wire) or to Frank Phillips (Sun).
No trial for Dempsey's killing appears in the coverage.
